stories.title: Samsung Expands AirDrop Support to the Galaxy A56 With One UI 9
stories.description: The post Samsung Expands AirDrop Support to the Galaxy A56 With One UI 9 appeared first on Android Headlines. Swapping high-resolution photos and videos between Android and Apple devices has long been a frustrating mess of compressed messaging apps and temporary cloud links. The new One UI 9 update completely changes that dynamic for Galaxy A56 owners by bringing native AirDrop compatibility to Samsung‘s mid-range lineup. That means you can now send files straight to nearby iPhones without jumping through extra technical hoops. A direct connection between Galaxy and Apple hardware The One UI 9 brings a new setting called “Share with Apple devices” to the Galaxy A56’s Quick Share menu. Toggling this option lets your phone scan for nearby iPhones, iPads, and Mac computers to send and receive media seamlessly. The entire transfer happens locally over wireless signals, keeping your files private and preserving original image resolution (via SammyGuru). This cross-platform feature builds on a broader effort by Google and Samsung to integrate AirDrop protocols into Android’s native Quick Share system. Samsung initially debuted the trick on flagship hardware like the Galaxy S26 series earlier this year. Bringing the exact same capability to the Galaxy A56 shows that budget-friendly phones are no longer left behind when it comes to major software perks. Setup requirements and real-world transfer speeds To start sharing files across platforms, the receiving Apple device simply needs its AirDrop visibility set to “Everyone.” Once that is toggled, the Galaxy A56 detects the target hardware inside the standard Quick Share sheet just like any other nearby Android device. Accepting the prompt on the Apple display begins the transfer instantly over local Bluetooth and Wi-Fi channels. Samsung does point out a couple of minor performance caveats during cross-platform transfers. Your Galaxy A56 might temporarily disconnect from active Wi-Fi networks while searching for nearby Apple devices or completing a heavy file send. Speeds can also run slightly slower than sharing between two Samsung devices, but skipping compression apps makes that small delay worthwhile. Erasing file sharing headaches for everyday users The rollout on the Galaxy A56 follows a similar expansion to the Galaxy S25 FE under One UI 9. Extending this functionality beyond $1,000 flagship devices removes one of the most persistent headaches for mixed-platform families and group chats. stories.title: Apple Acquires Assets of AI Audio Startup Samplab
stories.description: Apple has acquired certain assets of Zurich-based Samplab, whose AI tools let musicians edit recorded audio like MIDI, and is hiring some of its staff. The deal, dated June 17, surfaced Oct. 19 on the EU's Digital Markets Act acquisitions list. Logic Pro already has stem splitting; Samplab's polyphonic note editing would be new. Apple has bought certain assets of Samplab GmbH, a Zurich-based startup whose software let musicians edit recorded audio as if it were MIDI. The deal came to light on Oct. 19, 2026, when the European Union's list of acquisitions under the Digital Markets Act was updated with an entry dated June 17, AppleInsider reported. According to the filing quoted by 9to5Mac, Apple, "through a subsidiary, will acquire certain assets of Samplab GmbH ('Samplab') and offer employment to and hire certain Samplab employees." The filing doesn't disclose financial terms or how many people Apple is hiring. Samplab pitched itself as "music production for the age of AI." Its website called the product an "ultimate audio editor for musicians" that let creators "edit audio files as if you were working with MIDI." MacRumors said the company sold a desktop app and plugins for converting audio to MIDI, detecting and editing chords, stem splitting, and editing notes in polyphonic audio without affecting the timbre of the original. The site also promised to match the tempo and key of samples so they sound good together. What it could add to Logic Pro Samplab's plugins worked inside digital audio workstations, Logic Pro among them. Logic Pro already has Stem Splitter, which arrived in 2024, and Chord ID, but MacRumors noted that polyphonic note editing would be new. AppleInsider expects the technology to land in Logic Pro and Apple Creator Studio, though neither Apple nor Samplab has commented. The startup was founded in 2020 by Manuel Fritsche and Gian-Marco Hutter and is believed to have had no more than 10 employees, according to AppleInsider. Samplab told users in late June that it was closing and would refund the remainder of annual subscriptions; MacRumors puts the shutdown date at Sept. 17. Its website now redirects to apple.com, and its YouTube channel has been emptied of videos. The arrangement looks a lot like Apple's deal with personalized audio startup Huxe, which the EU list revealed earlier in October. In that case Apple agreed to make employment offers to "certain employees of Huxe AI" and to "receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe's intellectual property rights," TechCrunch reported. Most of the deals Apple has reported to the EU involve small firms like Samplab, Huxe and Prompt AI. The big exception is Q.ai, which Apple bought in January 2026 for an estimated $2 billion.

Apple Caps iPhone Duo Preorders at Two to Stop Resale Scalpers
stories.description: The post Apple Caps iPhone Duo Preorders at Two to Stop Resale Scalpers appeared first on Android Headlines. Getting your hands on Apple‘s first foldable phone is turning out to be a real test of patience. Preorders for the iPhone Duo opened just a few days ago, and shipping estimates slipped into early next year almost instantly. To keep resellers from buying up all available stock and flipping the hardware for crazy markups, Apple is officially capping orders at two units per customer. If you try to add a third phone to your cart on Apple’s online store, a warning message pops up right away. The notification asks you to adjust your total quantity down to two before you can proceed to checkout. Stopping resellers as online prices soar The new purchase restriction is already live across Apple’s web stores in the US, the UK, Japan, and Spain. Tech outlets like Engadget and MacRumors verified the rule across multiple regions, confirming that the two-unit limit applies to every color and storage configuration. Apple stepped in after scalpers started listing fresh preorders on sites like eBay for wild prices. Some listings are asking for over $5,000 for a phone that officially starts at $1,999, taking advantage of buyers who want the hardware on day one. Long wait times and alternative buying options Placing an order directly through Apple right now means your phone won’t arrive until late January. That long wait is frustrating for anyone excited about the new hardware, but paying thousands extra to a random reseller on the internet is a huge gamble. If you want to grab an iPhone Duo sooner without paying scalper prices, checking third-party options is your best bet. Major wireless carriers and electronics retailers like Best Buy still offer earlier pickup and delivery dates for specific models, though available stock changes quickly. A familiar move for high demand launches Limiting how many devices one person can buy isn’t a new play for Apple. The company has used similar checkout caps during previous high-demand hardware debuts in China and earlier US iPhone launches to give regular shoppers a fair shot. While determined resellers often try to get around these rules using multiple credit cards and different shipping addresses, capping cart totals slows down bulk buying. For regular customers, ordering through official channels ensures you pay standard retail price, even if you have to wait for shipping. The post Apple Caps iPhone Duo Preorders at Two to Stop Resale Scalpers appeared first on Android Headlines.
